Rendering and inspection tools were available in the local environment. Following revised instructions, inspection rose to 97%, PDF black-square artifacts disappeared, and PowerPoint formatting errors fell to 64%. reasoning: The classification survives note 3: the best-supported omission is not looking at reachable visual evidence before submitting files, rather than an established inability to reason through the task. Under note 8, visible defects were discoverable through reasonable inspection; the absence of an explicit initial rendering checklist does not establish an instruction–grader mismatch. Note 11 does not support Satisficing because the source documents insufficient inspection, not deliberate effort-minimizing early stopping. Note 12 provides no stronger alternative because no missed persistent instruction file is identified; likewise, no explicit ignored tool response or upstream service failure is documented. Observation Failure remains the strongest fit, but confidence is medium because aggregate improvements after several simultaneous changes do not establish a unique root cause for every affected run.

## Scope of the source

I read **§3.4 and Appendix A.3 of the GDPval paper**, along with the relevant evaluation-method and tool-environment details. **These sections do not describe one identifiable agent run.** They report observations across multiple GPT-5 runs and a subsequent experiment with revised instructions and scaffolding. They contain no individual task transcript, sequence of tool calls, or before-and-after deliverables.

The chronological account below therefore describes the documented evaluation sequence, distinguishing observed behavior from instructions the researchers later supplied.

## 1. The agent received professional work requests and supporting files

GPT-5 was evaluated on GDPval tasks: requests for professional work products, often accompanied by reference files. The gold subset contained 220 tasks across 44 occupations. Tasks could require documents, slide decks, spreadsheets, and other digital deliverables—not simply a textual answer.

The paper describes these tasks as **precisely specified, one-shot, and noninteractive**, with the task context provided in the prompt. Thus, this was not a documented conversation in which a user repeatedly reviewed drafts and requested corrections. The cited sections do not identify a particular request, occupation, reference file, or filename associated with the reported formatting problems. [1, §§2.3, 5]

For OpenAI models, the evaluation environment enabled **web search and the code interpreter**, with background sampling. It also supplied file-processing libraries and additional packages, including LibreOffice; the models were told about the additional packages. Appendix A.6.4 lists tools for working with PDFs, Word documents, PowerPoint files, spreadsheets, and images. This establishes what was available, but not which library or command any particular run used. [1, §3.1, footnote 2; Appendix A.6.4]

## 2. GPT-5 produced deliverables, but visual inspection was uncommon in the initial condition

The initial runs produced files that the researchers could evaluate. Section 3.4 reports that agents used their multimodal capabilities to **inspect deliverables in only 15% of cases** before the prompting change.

The paper does not provide the underlying inspection calls. It does not show an individual agent rendering a document, opening an image, noticing a problem, or deciding to submit anyway. Nor does it establish that runs without multimodal inspection performed no other checks. The observable statement is narrower: visual inspection, as measured by the researchers, occurred at the reported 15% rate. [1, §3.4]

## 3. Submitted files contained visible problems

The researchers reported two concrete observations about the initial outputs:

- **More than half of generated PDFs contained black-square artifacts.**
- **86% of PowerPoint files contained what the paper calls “egregious formatting errors.”**

These were problems present in generated deliverables, not merely hypothetical concerns in a checklist. However, the cited sections do not reproduce an affected PDF page or slide, identify the text replaced by a black square, or specify the layout defect in an individual presentation. It would therefore go beyond the source to describe a particular clipped heading, overlapping chart, or missing glyph as the event in this case. [1, §3.4]

In the wider evaluation, occupational experts compared unlabeled model and human deliverables against the request and reference files, then provided preferences and detailed justifications. Section 3.3 reports that formatting was the principal reported reason GPT-5-high deliverables lost to human deliverables. **This was evaluation feedback collected by the researchers; the paper does not say that these judgments were returned to the same agent runs for revision.** [1, §§2.5, 3.3]

## 4. Researchers introduced more explicit production and checking instructions

After observing these results, the researchers created a general-purpose prompt intended to improve deliverable quality. Appendix A.3 reproduces that prompt, lightly edited to omit some details of the scaffolding setup.

The revised instructions addressed file creation and rendering directly. Among other requirements, they told the agent to:

- Avoid the nonbreaking hyphen `U+2011`, using the ordinary hyphen `U+002D` instead.
- Avoid emojis, nonstandard bullets, and other special characters unless strongly justified.
- Use **LibreOffice to create PDFs**.
- Use broadly available fonts, recommending Noto Sans or Noto Serif, and embed alternative fonts when necessary.
- Keep graphics legible and appropriately sized.
- Put requested deliverables in files in the container rather than only in the final message.
- Keep the submission message concise and disclose any portion of the task that could not be completed. [1, Appendix A.3]

The prompt also prescribed a five-step pre-submission procedure:

1. **Convert visual deliverables into PNG images**, with a separate image for each page or slide.
2. **Display and inspect those images**, checking for cut-off, overlapping, distorted, blank, or difficult-to-read content.
3. **Write programmatic formatting checks** for highly visual submissions, including checks for blank pages, off-page content, unintended overlap, and page or slide limits.
4. **Summarize the requested deliverables and match each requirement to the produced work.**
5. **Open and check the final submission files**, ensuring that only the intended files were included and that they were not corrupted.

If a check revealed a formatting problem, the agent was instructed to fix it and repeat all five steps. The prompt emphasized going page by page or slide by slide and required a final `CONFIDENCE[XX]` statement. [1, Appendix A.3]

**These are documented instructions, not a transcript showing that every subsequent run completed every step.** The paper reports increased visual inspection, but does not give per-step compliance results.

## 5. The researchers also changed the surrounding execution and selection setup

Section 3.4 reports two additional scaffolding changes:

- Enabling **GET requests inside the container**.
- Performing **best-of-four sampling** with a GPT-5 judge.

Appendix A.3 explains the latter: the judge received the task prompt, reference files, and deliverable files from four submissions and was asked to choose the best. This was a selection procedure across candidate submissions, not a documented sequence in which one agent received critiques and repaired the same file four times. [1, §3.4; Appendix A.3]

## 6. Subsequent runs improved, but substantial PowerPoint problems remained

The paper reports these before-and-after results:

| Reported observation | Initial condition | Revised-prompt condition |
|---|---:|---:|
| Use of multimodal capabilities to inspect deliverables | 15% | 97% |
| Black-square artifacts in generated PDFs | More than half of PDFs | Eliminated in the reported responses |
| Egregious formatting errors in PowerPoint files | 86% | 64% |

Section 3.4 also reports a **five-percentage-point improvement in human-preference win rates** from prompting. [1, §3.4]

The final documented outcome is therefore an improvement across subsequent runs, not a verified repair of one specific submission. PDF black-square artifacts disappeared in the reported experiment, and visual inspection became much more common. Nevertheless, **64% of PowerPoint files still contained the reported serious formatting problems**.

The source does not disclose the individual commands, runtime warnings, screenshots, final messages, or confidence scores behind these aggregate results. It supports this chronological account of initial submissions, researcher observations, revised instructions, and subsequent outcomes—but not a more granular reconstruction of a single agent’s actions.

## Scope of the source

I read **§3.4 and Appendix A.3 of the GDPval paper**, along with the relevant evaluation-method and tool-environment details. **These sections do not describe one identifiable agent run.** They report observations across multiple GPT-5 runs and a subsequent experiment with revised instructions and scaffolding. They contain no individual task transcript, sequence of tool calls, or before-and-after deliverables.

The chronological account below therefore describes the documented evaluation sequence, distinguishing observed behavior from instructions the researchers later supplied.

## 1. The agent received professional work requests and supporting files

GPT-5 was evaluated on GDPval tasks: requests for professional work products, often accompanied by reference files. The gold subset contained 220 tasks across 44 occupations. Tasks could require documents, slide decks, spreadsheets, and other digital deliverables—not simply a textual answer.

The paper describes these tasks as **precisely specified, one-shot, and noninteractive**, with the task context provided in the prompt. Thus, this was not a documented conversation in which a user repeatedly reviewed drafts and requested corrections. The cited sections do not identify a particular request, occupation, reference file, or filename associated with the reported formatting problems. [1, §§2.3, 5]

For OpenAI models, the evaluation environment enabled **web search and the code interpreter**, with background sampling. It also supplied file-processing libraries and additional packages, including LibreOffice; the models were told about the additional packages. Appendix A.6.4 lists tools for working with PDFs, Word documents, PowerPoint files, spreadsheets, and images. This establishes what was available, but not which library or command any particular run used. [1, §3.1, footnote 2; Appendix A.6.4]

## 2. GPT-5 produced deliverables, but visual inspection was uncommon in the initial condition

The initial runs produced files that the researchers could evaluate. Section 3.4 reports that agents used their multimodal capabilities to **inspect deliverables in only 15% of cases** before the prompting change.

The paper does not provide the underlying inspection calls. It does not show an individual agent rendering a document, opening an image, noticing a problem, or deciding to submit anyway. Nor does it establish that runs without multimodal inspection performed no other checks. The observable statement is narrower: visual inspection, as measured by the researchers, occurred at the reported 15% rate. [1, §3.4]

## 3. Submitted files contained visible problems

The researchers reported two concrete observations about the initial outputs:

- **More than half of generated PDFs contained black-square artifacts.**
- **86% of PowerPoint files contained what the paper calls “egregious formatting errors.”**

These were problems present in generated deliverables, not merely hypothetical concerns in a checklist. However, the cited sections do not reproduce an affected PDF page or slide, identify the text replaced by a black square, or specify the layout defect in an individual presentation. It would therefore go beyond the source to describe a particular clipped heading, overlapping chart, or missing glyph as the event in this case. [1, §3.4]

In the wider evaluation, occupational experts compared unlabeled model and human deliverables against the request and reference files, then provided preferences and detailed justifications. Section 3.3 reports that formatting was the principal reported reason GPT-5-high deliverables lost to human deliverables. **This was evaluation feedback collected by the researchers; the paper does not say that these judgments were returned to the same agent runs for revision.** [1, §§2.5, 3.3]
